'''''Handroanthus''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Bignoniaceae]].<ref name="mabberley2008">David J. Mabberley. 2008. ''Mabberley's Plant-Book'' third edition (2008). Cambridge University Press: UK. {{ISBN|978-0-521-82071-4}}</ref> It consists of 30 [[species]] of [[tree]]s, known in [[Latin America]] by the [[common name]]s '''poui''', '''pau d'arco''', or '''ipê'''. The latter sometimes appears as '''epay''' or simply '''ipe'''{{pron}} (unaccented) in [[English language|English]]. The large [[timber]] species are sometimes called '''lapacho''' or '''guayacan''', but these names are more properly applied to the species ''[[Handroanthus lapacho]]'' and ''[[Handroanthus guayacan]]'', respectively.

The [[Botanical name|name]] ''Handroanthus'' was [[valid publication|established]] in 1970,<ref name="ipnihandroanthus">''Handroanthus'' in International Plant Names Index. (see ''External links'' below).</ref> but was not generally accepted. In 1992, its species were included in ''[[Tabebuia]]'' in the most recent revision of that genus.<ref name="gentry1992fn">Alwyn H. Gentry. 1992. "Bignoniaceae: Part II (Tribe Tecomeae)". ''Flora Neotropica'' Monograph '''25'''(part 2):1-150.</ref> ''Handroanthus'' was [[Resurrection (taxonomy)|resurrected]] in 2007 when a comparison of [[DNA sequence]]s by [[cladistic]] methods showed that ''Tabebuia'', as then [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscribed]], was not [[monophyletic]].<ref name="grose2007phylogeny">Susan O. Grose and Richard G. Olmstead. 2007. "Evolution of a Charismatic Neotropical Clade: Molecular Phylogeny of ''Tabebuia'' s.l., Crescentieae, and Allied Genera (Bignoniaceae)". ''Systematic Botany'' '''32'''(3):650-659.</ref><ref name="grose2007revisions">Susan O. Grose and Richard G. Olmstead. 2007. "Taxonomic Revisions in the Polyphyletic Genus ''Tabebuia'' s.l. (Bignoniaceae)". ''Systematic Botany'' '''32'''(3):660-670.</ref>

''Handroanthus'' are [[Indigenous (ecology)|indigenous]] from [[Central America]] to northern [[Argentina]], [[Paraguay]], [[Brazil]], and [[Chile]], with one species, ''[[Handroanthus billbergii]]'', native to northern [[South America]] and the [[Antilles]]. ''Handroanthus'' are frequently [[Gardening|cultivated]] far from their [[Nature|natural]] [[Range (biology)|range]], as [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] trees, for their large and showy flowers. They easily become [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] where [[Introduced species|introduced]] because their seeds are prolifically produced and widely [[Anemochory|scattered by the wind]].<ref name="staples2005">George W. Staples and Derral R. Herbst. 2005. "A Tropical Garden Flora" Bishop Museum Press: Honolulu, HI, USA. {{ISBN|978-1-58178-039-0}}</ref> Several species are important timber trees of the [[Americas|American]] [[tropics]].<ref name="gentry1992ambg">Alwyn H. Gentry. 1992. "A Synopsis of Bignoniaceae Ethnobotany and Economic Botany". ''Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden'' '''79'''(1):53-64.</ref> [[Herbal medicine|Medicinal use]] has been reported, but its [[efficacy]] and [[side effects]] have not been well studied.

== Description ==
The following description is excerpted from the [[Scientific paper|paper]] that resurrected ''Handroanthus'' in 2007.<ref name="grose2007revisions"/>

* [[Tree]]s or occasionally [[shrub]]s.
* [[Wood]] is very dense. [[Wood#Heartwood and sapwood|Heartwood]] distinct from [[Glossary of botanical terms#sapwood|sapwood]], olive brown to black, [[lapachol]] present in large quantities.
* [[Leaf|Leaves]] [[Leaf shape|palmately]] (3)5-9_[[Leaf#Divisions of the blade|foliate]].
* [[Leaflet (botany)|Leaflets]] with various types of [[trichome]]s as well as [[Glossary of botanical terms#lepidote|lepidote]] [[Indumentum|scales]].
* [[Inflorescence]] with [[dichotomous branching]].
* [[Calyx (botany)|Calyx]] [[Glossary of botanical terms#coriaceous|coriaceous]], [[Glossary of botanical terms#campanulate|campanulate]], 5 dentate, [[pubescent (botany)|pubescent]].
* [[Corolla (flower)|Corolla]] tubular, [[yellow]] or [[magenta]] with yellow throat.
* [[Stamen]]s [[Stamen#Descriptive terms|didynamous]]; [[Theca]]e [[divaricate]]; [[Staminode]] reduced.
* [[Ovary (plants)|Ovary]] [[Cone|conical]] to [[Glossary of botanical terms#linear|linear]], [[Locule|bilocular]].
* [[Ovule]]s in 2 to 10 series in each [[locule]].
* [[Fruit]] an elongate [[Dehiscence (botany)|dehiscent]] [[Capsule (fruit)|capsule]].
* [[Seed]]s thin with 2 [[Glossary of botanical terms#W|wings]]. Wings thin and sharply demarcated from seed body.

''Handroanthus'' is distinguished from ''Tabebuia'' by several [[Plant morphology|morphological]] [[Phenotypic trait|characters]]. The wood is among the hardest and heaviest known. The heartwood is distinct from the sapwood and contains large quantities of lapachol. ''Handroanthus'' has the same lepidote scales as ''Tabebuia'', but also has various types of hair. The calyx is 5-dentate and campanulate to cupular. The corolla is yellow, except in those four species where it is magenta with a yellow throat. ''Tabebuia'' has only two yellow-flowered species, ''[[Tabebuia aurea]]'' and ''[[Tabebuia nodosa]]''. The fruit of ''Handroanthus'' is rarely [[Glabrousness|glabrous]] like that of ''Tabebuia''. It usually ranges from sparsely pubescent to densely [[tomentose]].

== Uses ==
''Handroanthus'' is widely used as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental tree]] in the tropics in [[landscaping]] gardens, public squares, and boulevards due to its impressive and colorful flowering. Many flowers appear on still-leafless stems at the end of the [[dry season]], making the [[Anthesis|floral display]] more conspicuous. ''[[Handroanthus impetiginosus]]'', ''[[Handroanthus chrysotrichus]]'', and ''[[Handroanthus ochraceus]]'' are well-known throughout the [[tropics]].<ref name="staples2005"/> ''[[Handroanthus chrysanthus]]'', ''[[Handroanthus guayacan]]'', ''[[Handroanthus serratifolius]]'', ''[[Handroanthus umbellatus]]'', and ''[[Handroanthus vellosoi]]'' are also [[Plant propagation|planted]] in [[Köppen climate classification|warm climate]]s.<ref name="rhs">[[Anthony Huxley]], Mark Griffiths, and Margot Levy (1992). ''The New Royal Horticultural Society Dictionary of Gardening''. The Macmillan Press, Limited: London. The Stockton Press: New York. {{ISBN|978-0-333-47494-5}} (set).</ref>

''[[Handroanthus heptaphyllus]]'', ''Handroanthus serratifolius'', ''Handroanthus guayacan'', ''Handroanthus chrysanthus'', and ''[[Handroanthus billbergii]]'' are important timber trees of the [[Neotropical realm|Neotropics]].<ref name="gentry1992ambg"/> The wood of ''Handroanthus billbergii'' is valued for [[Wood carving|carving]].<ref name="mabberley2008"/> Indigenous peoples of the Amazon made hunting bows from the wood, which is the source of the common name ''pau d'arco'', "bow stick".<ref>{{cite book|title=Tapping the Green Market: Certification and Management of Non-timber Forest Products|year=1986|publisher=Earthscan Publications|location=London|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QTKxUhTugwUC&q=tabebuia+bow&pg=PA85|author=M. Costanza von der Pahlen|editor1=Patricia Shanley |editor2=Alan R. Pierce |editor3=Sarah A. Laird |editor4=Abraham Guillan |access-date=12 April 2012|page=85|chapter=Chapter 7. Pau d'arco (''Tabebuia'' spp.)|isbn=9781853838712}}</ref>

Much of the [[lumber]] from ''Handroanthus'' is [[export]]ed. The wood is durable outdoors, where it is usually used for [[furniture]] and [[deck (building)|decking]]. It is increasingly popular as a decking material due to its [[Plant defense against herbivory|insect resistance]] and durability. ''Handroanthus'' and the unrelated ''[[Guaiacum]]'' ([[Zygophyllaceae]]) produce the hardest, heaviest, and most durable wood of the American tropics.<ref name="gentry1992ambg"/> Dead trees of ''Handroanthus guayacan'' remain standing after they were killed by flooding of their [[habitat]] during construction of the [[Panama Canal]].<ref name="mabberley2008"/>

The wood of ''Handroanthus'' brings a high [[price]]. The wood of other species is sometimes [[fraud]]ulently sold as ''Handroanthus''. By 2007, [[Forest Stewardship Council|FSC]]-certified ipê wood had become readily available on the market, although certificates are occasionally forged.<ref>FSC Watch: {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20090629111603/http://www.fsc-watch.org/archives/2007/08/22/SmartWood_misled_US_local_authority_over_FSC_timber SmartWood misled US local authority over FSC timber]}}. Posted 2007-AUG-22. Retrieved 2008-JAN-27.</ref>

Much of the ipê imported into the United States is used for decking. Starting in the late 1960s, [[importer|importing companies]] targeted large [[boardwalk]] projects to sell ipê, beginning with the [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]], which maintains the city's [[boardwalk]]s, including along the [[beach]] of [[Coney Island]]. The city began using ipê around that time and has since converted the entire boardwalk—over {{Convert|10|mi|km|abbr=on}} long—to ipê. The ipê lasted about 25 years, at which time (1994) the department began replacing it with new ipê. ''[[La Sultana]]'', a yacht refashioned from a Soviet spy vessel, was fitted with an ipê deck during its restoration.<ref name = bil>[http://www.billionaire.com/yachts-boats/2106/la-sultanasuperyacht-the-spy-ship-you-can-sunbathe-on La Sultana Superyacht: The Spy Ship You Can Sunbathe On].  Billionaire. 14 September 2015. Tara Loader Wilkinson. 24 December 2015.</ref> In 2008-2009, [[Wildwood, New Jersey]], rebuilt a section of its boardwalk using ipê. The town had pledged to use domestic [[black locust]], but it was not available in time.<ref>{{cite news |title=Wildwood Opts for Ipe Wood Over Black Locust in Boardwalk Construction |url=http://www.capemaycountyherald.com/article/38282-wildwood-opts-ipe-wood-over-black-locust-boardwalk-construction |work=[[Cape May County Herald]] |date=March 17, 2009 |access-date=2009-03-17 |archive-date=2011-09-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928064650/http://www.capemaycountyherald.com/article/38282-wildwood-opts-ipe-wood-over-black-locust-boardwalk-construction |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Given that ipê trees typically grow in [[Population density|densities]] of only one or two trees per {{convert|1|acre|ha}}, large areas of [[forest]] must be searched and cut down to create paths to [[Harvesting|harvest]] the trees to fill orders for boardwalks and to a lesser extent, homeowner [[Deck (building)|decks]].

The bark of several species of ''Handroanthus'' is sold in South American markets. Similar-looking bark is often fraudulently passed off as ''Handroanthus''. It is used in various ways to relieve certain [[symptom]]s of certain [[cancer]]s.<ref name="gentry1992ambg"/> No evidence shows that it prevents the disease or slows its progression, as is often claimed.

The bark is dried, shredded, and then boiled to make a bitter or sour-tasting brownish-colored tea. Tea from the [[Bark (botany)|inner bark]] of pink ipê (''[[Handroanthus impetiginosus]]'') is known as pau d'arco, [[lapacho]], or taheebo.

''[[Handroanthus ochraceus]]'' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]]: ''Tabebuia heteropoda''), ''[[Handroanthus incanus]]'', and other species are occasionally used as an [[Food additive|additive]] to the [[entheogen]]ic drink [[Ayahuasca]].<ref>Jonathan Ott. 1995. In: Ayahuasca Analogues: Pangaean Entheogens.</ref>

== Ecology ==
The [[nectar]] of ''Handroanthus'' flowers is an important food source for several species of [[bees]] and [[hummingbird]]s.<ref name="revista2005">{{cite journal |author1=Luciana Baza Mendonça |author2=Luiz dos Anjos |year=2005 |title=Beija-flores (Aves, Trochilidae) e seus recursos florais em uma área urbana do Sul do Brasil |trans-title=Hummingbirds (Aves, Trochilidae) and their flowers in an urban area of southern Brazil |language=pt |journal=[[Revista Brasileira de Zoologia]] |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=51–59 |doi=10.1590/S0101-81752005000100007 |url=http://www.scielo.br/pdf/rbzool/v22n1/a07v22n1.pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref>

''[[Mycosphaerella tabebuiae]]'', a [[plant]] [[pathogenic]] [[sac fungus]] was first discovered on a ''Handroanthus'' tree, known at that time as ''Tabebuia''.{{Citation needed|date=February 2013}} The [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomy]] of [[Mycosphaerella]] is in much confusion and the recognition of this name is questionable.{{Citation needed|date=February 2013}}

== Symbolism ==
Because of its popularity, ''Handroanthus'' has often been adopted as a [[symbol]] or [[emblem]] for [[Sovereign state|nations]] or other [[political division]]s.

The distinction between [[Floral emblem|national flower]] and [[List of national trees|national tree]] is sometimes not entirely clear. Gentry (1992) gives the following information without making that distinction.<ref name="gentry1992ambg"/>

* [[Brazil]] - ''Handroanthus serratifolius''
* [[Ecuador]] - ''Handroanthus chrysanthus''
* [[Paraguay]] - ''Handroanthus heptaphyllus''
* [[Venezuela]] - ''Handroanthus billbergii''

== History ==
[[File:Araguaney.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Araguaney (''[[Handroanthus chrysanthus]]'') tree on a [[Caracas]] street]]
[[File:Tabebuia impetiginosa hojas.jpeg|thumb|right|Leaves of pink ipê (''[[Handroanthus impetiginosus]]'') in detail]]

The genus ''Handroanthus'' was erected by [[Joáo Rodrigues de Mattos]] in 1970.<ref name="mattos1970">Joáo Rodrigues de Mattos. 1970. "''Handroanthus'', Um novo gênero para os "ipês" do Brasil". ''Loefgrenia'' '''50''': 1-4.</ref> It was [[Eponym|named]] for the [[Brazilian people|Brazilian]] [[botanist]] [[Oswaldo Handro]]. "Anthus" is [[Etymology|derived]] from a [[Greek language|Greek]] word for "flower".{{Citation needed|date=February 2013}}

Most botanists at that time did not agree with the [[Segregate (taxonomy)|separation]] of ''Handroanthus'' from ''Tabebuia''. [[Alwyn Howard Gentry|Alwyn H. Gentry]] objected strenuously and warned against "succumbing to further paroxysms of unwarranted splitting".<ref name="gentry1972">Alwyn H. Gentry. 1972. "''Handroanthus'' (Bignoniaceae): A critique". ''Taxon'' '''21'''(1):113-114.</ref>

In 1992, Gentry published a full [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] [[Treatise|treatment]] of ''Tabebuia'', in which he [[Diagnosis (taxonomy)|described]] 99 species and one [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] for the genus.<ref name="gentry1992fn"/> These consist of the 67 species and one hybrid that remain in ''Tabebuia'', the two species transferred to ''[[Roseodendron]]'', and the 30 species that are now placed in ''Handroanthus''. Gentry divided ''Tabebuia'' into 10 species groups. ''Handroanthus'', as it is currently [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscribed]], is composed of Gentry's groups 3, 4, and 5. Gentry believed group 5 to be [[Nature|natural]], while groups 3 and 4 were artificial, designated for the sole purpose of easier [[Identification (biology)|identification]].

In 2007, a [[molecular phylogenetic]] [[Research|study]] resolved ''Tabebuia'' as consisting of three [[Resampling (statistics)|strongly supported]] [[clade]]s, none of which was [[sister taxon|sister]] to either of the others.<ref name="grose2007phylogeny"/> Thus ''Tabebuia'' was shown to be [[polyphyletic]]. One of these clades consisted of the two species that constitute the genus ''[[Roseodendron]]''. Another contained the [[type species]] for ''Tabebuia'', and consequently retained that [[Genus#Generic name|name]]. The [[Botanical name|name]] ''Handroanthus'' was resurrected for the third clade, which contained its [[Biological type|type]] species, ''[[Handroanthus albus]]''.<ref name="grose2007revisions"/>

''Handroanthus'' is sister to a clade consisting of ''[[Spirotecoma]]'', ''[[Parmentiera]]'', ''[[Crescentia]]'', and ''[[Amphitecna]]''. It had for a long time been placed in the [[Tribe (biology)|tribe]] [[Tecomeae]], but that tribe has been greatly reduced to only 11 or 12 genera and no longer includes ''Handroanthus''. ''Handroanthus'' is one of the 12 to 14 genera that make up a [[Taxon|group]] informally known as the ''Tabebuia'' alliance.<ref name="olmstead2009">Richard G. Olmstead, Michelle L. Zjhra, Lúcia G. Lohmann, Susan O. Grose, and Andrew J. Eckert. 2009. "A molecular phylogeny and classification of Bignoniaceae". ''American Journal of Botany'' '''96'''(9): 1731–1743. {{doi|10.3732/ajb.0900004}}</ref> This group has not been assigned to any [[taxonomic rank]], and neither has [[Crescentiina]], the smallest group that it is a member of.

[[Cladistic]] analysis of [[DNA]] data has strongly supported ''Handroanthus'', but sampling of taxa and DNA has not been sufficient to strongly support any relationships within the genus.
